articles.title: Introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen for Agentic Workflows
articles.text:
Introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen

Hydrogen brings cutting-edge intelligence to everyone.

Your browser does not support the audio element.

Listen to article

[[duration]] minutes

This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental

Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen, bringing cutting-edge intelligence to everyone — with speed and efficiency for everyday coding and agentic workflows.While our frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon, excel at deep, long-horizon reasoning on your hardest problems, Hydrogen is built for rapid execution across diverse agentic workflows. With Hydrogen, we’re also bringing Gemini 4 to everyone — for all tiers of Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, Gemini for business, the Gemini app, Google Search, and paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity.Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class. Gemini 4 Hydrogen is priced flat across its entire 1 million-token context window at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.

Unlocking efficiencies in multi-model workloadsIn real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows.To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity. Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster. For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs.

Scaling developer and enterprise workflows

Beyond multi-model workflows, Hydrogen is a major standalone upgrade for teams migrating from Gemini 3.8 Flash. It delivers significant leaps in both speed and intelligence — finishing tasks 2.5 times faster at its high default setting while more than tripling Terminal-Bench 4.1 scores (57% vs. 18.2%), cutting fabricated claims by more than 5x, and adapting cleanly when a tool call fails or a search returns empty. It also matches or outperforms competing models in its class across core developer and enterprise workflows:Iterative repository coding and debugging: Hydrogen handles issue resolution, debugging, rapid iteration, and codebase Q&A with focused, surgical edits — delivering cleaner, production-ready code without rewriting unrelated files. It outperforms similar-tier models on SWE-sweep where it has to discover and repair bugs without breaking existing code. To explore large repositories efficiently, the model excels at natively batching file-read and search calls in parallel rather than inspecting files one by one; in early testing across complex graphs, SQL, and data-heavy enterprise workflows, our partners have seen Hydrogen run 2x to 2.8x faster while reducing token usage by 12% to 23%, compared to 3.8 Flash.Open-ended agentic execution: On multi-step tasks like deep research, data analysis, and broad codebase navigation, Hydrogen ranks #5 on Agent Arena, arena.ai’s live benchmark. For deep domain reasoning and analysis, it leads its class on HLE-Diamond (58.8%), ranks #1 overall on Vals Tax Agent Bench (52.3%), ties for #1 on the Vals Legal Research Bench (55.8%), and leads its class on AutomationBench-AA.

Multimodal knowledge work: Hydrogen pairs native 1 million-token input with up to 1 million output tokens to synthesize dense PDFs, spreadsheets, charts, audio, and recorded video into polished, cited reports and structured deliverables. It outperforms other models on the new Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark (53.4%) for end-to-end agentic knowledge work over complex visual files, and on Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 (71.6%) for end-to-end professional workflows.Web development: On tasks where speed matters to developers, like live UI prototyping, design-to-code iteration, and interactive app building, Hydrogen generates more functional, feature-complete layouts in fewer prompts.

Adaptable speed and intelligence across four thinking levels

We built Gemini 4 Hydrogen for real-world usability. Hydrogen’s four thinking levels — low, medium, high (default), and a new xhigh tier — offer a wide range of options across quality, latency, and cost, scaling in a smooth, predictable progression so you only wait and pay for the reasoning depth a task requires. Across thinking levels, Hydrogen matches or outperforms some of the competing models in its class while often finishing tasks faster and using fewer output tokens.

Fast, everyday help in the Gemini app and SearchFor consumers, Gemini 4 Hydrogen makes it easier to get things done, staying on track and following instructions more closely across multi-turn conversations.In the Gemini app, Hydrogen makes your everyday assistant even more helpful — it’s better at following your guidance, calling the right tools, and getting you to a reliable output with less back-and-forth.Ready-to-go writing, research, and everyday work: Hydrogen sticks closely to your tone, format, and specific rules, so email drafts, study guides, rewrites, and documents come back ready to use on the first try. When you are comparing products or synthesizing dense material, it pulls together clear tables and visual breakdowns without dropping key details.
Connects the dots and gets more tasks done: Hydrogen breaks down your goal step-by-step, pulling relevant context from your uploads, Google apps like Gmail and Google Drive, and Connected Apps like Airtable and Dropbox. When you start a task in Gemini, it also more frequently calls the right tools and skills for the job, helping save you time as you check things off your to-do list.
Everyday prototyping and iteration: For exploring and testing ideas, Hydrogen generates clean, working layouts in fewer prompts, making it easy to prototype and refine interactive projects quickly, like synthesizing real-time global lightning strike data into an interactive 3D globe.

Hydrogen is significantly upgrading Search, delivering more helpful, intuitive responses for all users globally.Better understands your true intent: With Hydrogen, you can ask your question in your natural flow of thought — even if you have multiple parts to your query, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests — and Search will intelligently comprehend what you’re looking for.More visual responses: You’ll get highly adaptive, visual, and easy-to-scan responses that are uniquely relevant to your needs, at the speed you expect from Search.Wider range of relevant links: With Hydrogen’s advanced reasoning, we’re also upgrading our query fan-out technique in Search, connecting you to a broader range of helpful links than before, helping you find sites you previously might not have discovered.

Designed for safe, dependable execution at scaleGemini 4 Hydrogen brings improvements from our latest Gemini 4 safety and security stack to our broadest audience yet, combining built-in training with real-time surface safeguards to help mitigate both misalignment and misuse. Beyond foundational protections, we focused on two areas that matter most for a faster model that’s for everyday work:Safe, aligned, and secure agentic workflows: While 3.8 Flash has strong alignment and safeguards, Hydrogen is a leap ahead. It reduces overreach in agentic tasks by up to 81% and under-service by up to 79%, and cuts misaligned actions and task shortcutting across tool-use and coding evaluations by 12x. When faced with impossible or blocked tasks, it is up to 2x less likely to bypass permission boundaries and achieves a 96.7% honesty rate on our internal agent honesty evaluation.Building on our commitment to reasoning transparency, Hydrogen also preserves 99.9% chain-of-thought legibility with zero deceptive reasoning edits across more than 200,000 audited turns. Against indirect prompt injection attacks, Hydrogen is more than 2.3x more resilient on the Gray Swan IPI benchmark, while significantly improving robustness across tool use, computer use, and coding agents.Helpful, reliable everyday interactions: Across our product surfaces, we tuned Hydrogen to make everyday conversations more reliable and safe. Our updated safeguards are also much more precise at distinguishing between real biosecurity risks and legitimate medical or scientific questions — keeping false refusals on HealthBench Pro under 0.4%.For more details see the Gemini 4 Hydrogen model card.

Gemini 4 Hydrogen, available to everyone todayStarting today, Hydrogen is rolling out globally across our developer, enterprise, and consumer surfaces:For developers: Build with the Gemini API in AI Studio and the paid tier in Android Studio, try it in AI Studio and if you’re a paid Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can try it in Google Antigravity.For enterprises: Deploy it in Gemini for business via the API or model drop down, Google Antigravity, and in Gemini in Google Sheets for eligible business subscriptions.For everyone: Start using it in the Gemini app model drop down

articles.sourceTitle: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers
articles.title: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers
articles.text:
United Airlines said on Wednesday that it is banning artificial intelligence agents from making flight reservations on behalf of travelers, citing security risks and the possibility that such actions could violate federal rules.Many consumers are turning to AI agents such as Meta's Muse and OpenAI's dots to complete tasks ranging from researching products and tracking down deals to making purchases.To make an airline booking, an AI agent requires access to a customer's personal information, including credentials like payment information. United has a problem with that, saying that "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles."The carrier also said that using an AI agent to, for example, check in for a flight could violate federal regulations, including rules requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage does not contain banned substances."As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants," said the airline, which is updating its booking and ticketing policies to reflect the new rule.United's new policy suggests the company wants to retain control over the customer booking process, said Henry Harteveldt, an aviation analyst at Atmosphere Research Group. "United is saying they don't want to add yet another, and potentially even more powerful, intermediary than they already face in terms of Google search, price-comparison metasearch sites and online travel agencies," he told CBS News. "Flight searches cost airlines money, and undoubtedly United wants to avoid the expense associated with the surge of AI bot flight searches."

Other airlines are taking a different tack to the emergence of AI agents. For example, Southwest has made its flight inventory viewable to ChatGPT users, who can access the airline's website through the AI app. United fares will continue to be bookable through flight aggregators such as Kayak, Hopper and Google Flights, Harteveldt said, adding that "consumers shouldn't find it any more difficult to find good fares on the airline.""But by blocking the AI bots, United won't make it any easier to find its fares, either," he said.

Edited by

Kris  Van Cleave

contributed to this report.

articles.title: Gemini Decisions API: Fast multimodal decisions
articles.text:
Gemini Decisions API: Fast, calibrated multimodal decisions

Introducing the Gemini Decisions API, powered by our new Gemini Decision 1 model. Evaluate up to 1,000 yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring questions in a fast, single pass across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs.

Felix Yu

Principal Scientist, Google DeepMind

Your browser does not support the audio element.

Listen to article

[[duration]] minutes

This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental

We are introducing the Gemini Decisions API to help you make fast, probabilistic choices across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. This tool computes confidence scores for multiple questions in a single pass, providing a cost-effective way to route queries, grade content, or check policy rules. You can start building today by accessing your API key in Google AI Studio and reviewing our documentation for Python, JavaScript, and REST guides.

Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental.

Today, we’re introducing the Gemini Decisions API, a new endpoint for fast, closed-set decisions powered by our new Gemini Decision 1 model (gemini-decision-1), available through the Gemini API in Google AI Studio.The Decisions API gives you purpose-built primitives for bounded choices like tool selection, policy checks, model routing, and context grading. You can pass one multimodal input across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs (up to 256K tokens) along with up to 1,000 independent questions. Rather than generating answer text token by token, Gemini Decision 1 scores your candidate options in a single forward pass, returning probabilities and confidence scores in 150-250 ms end-to-end latency at $0.10 per 1M input tokens with zero output tokens billed.

Strong performance and calibrationOn benchmarks spanning agent routing, reasoning, ranking, and multimodal understanding, Gemini Decision 1 leads across the suite, with the lowest calibration error.

Gemini Decision 1 scores options without token-by-token decoding, keeping median latency 50-100 ms of model compute (150-250 ms end-to-end), across multimodal inputs and contexts up to 16K tokens, remaining nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions per request. With zero output tokens billed, Gemini Decision 1 with the Decisions API is nearly 5x cheaper across the shared benchmark suite than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite with the Interactions API.Native multimodal evaluation across three decision types in one passBuilt on Gemini’s native multimodal architecture, Gemini Decision 1 can process text, images, audio, video, and PDFs directly in a single forward pass. You can combine modalities in one shared input, such as pairing a call recording with account metadata or a scanned PDF claim with damage photos, and tune resolution on image and video inputs to control visual detail and token cost.You can evaluate multiple questions against that shared input in a single request, mixing yes/no checks, multiple choice, and rubric scores. Every answer includes a confidence score (from 0 to 1) so your code can route ambiguous cases to a fallback or human reviewer:noul (Yes/No): Estimates the probability that a yes/no condition holds, with optional true and false description criteria.choice (Multiple Choice): Selects from 2 to 255 choices, returning the winner and normalized probabilities for every candidate.score (Ordered Rubric): Grades inputs across an ordered rubric (starting at 0), returning a continuous weighted score and per-level probabilities.The input field uses the same Content block format as the Interactions API. Here is how to check a photo of a breakroom counter, together with a text note, against all three question types in one request:

from google import genai

client = genai.Client(http_options={"api_version": "v1beta"})

result = client.decisions.create(
model="gemini-decision-1",
input=[{
"type": "image",
"uri": "https://storage.googleapis.com/generativeai-downloads/images/spill.jpg",
"mime_type": "image/jpeg",
},
{
"type": "text",
"text": "Breakroom counter check before the 9 AM client meeting.",
},
],
questions={
"has_spill": {
"type": "noul",
"instructions": "Is there an uncleaned liquid spill on the counter?",
},
"next_action": {
"type": "choice",
"instructions": "Which cleanup action fits the scene?",
"criteria": {
"wipe_with_cloth": "Small counter spill with a cloth or towel already nearby.",
"dispatch_janitorial": "Large floor hazard, broken glass, or active leak.",
"ready_for_meeting": "Counter is clean and ready.",
},
},
"severity": {
"type": "score",
"instructions": "Rate the severity of the counter mess.",
"criteria": [
"Clean and ready.",
"Minor localized spill.",
"Major spill or safety hazard.",
],
},
},
)

How teams are building with the Decisions APITeams across Google are already using the Decisions API as a low-latency control plane, shipping features simply by defining options rather than training custom classifiers or waiting on generative calls:Dynamic model routing in Gemini Notebook: Gemini Notebook uses the Decisions API as a real-time router to instantly direct incoming queries to the optimal model tier and thinking level for each request. The Decisions API classifies intent in milliseconds to serve everyday queries with up to 40% lower latency while reserving deep reasoning models for complex tasks.Rapid design iteration in Stitch: The new rapid canvas experiment in Stitch uses the Decisions API to generate playable wireframes of a product flow in seconds and to apply edits made by voice or tap almost instantly. When the flow feels right, one click hands the screens off to the full Stitch experience for deeper design polish.Emoji selection in CC: CC from Google Labs uses the Decisions API to pick the right emoji reaction from a palette of more than 200 options in a fraction of a second, so reactions appear instantly without adding latency.Safety layer for MCP tools in Search: Google Search uses the Decision API to detect adversarial behavior and content against adversarial evals with high efficacy within the latency envelope.

Stitch Rapid uses the Decisions API to design an entire product flow in seconds (1x speed).

Start building todayGemini Decision 1 is priced at $0.10 per 1M input tokens and $0 for output tokens, with an API no-cost tier you can use in Google AI Studio for prototyping. Your shared input is billed once per request no matter how many questions you evaluate (each question adds only its own instruction and criteria tokens). There are no output-token charges, variable thinking-token bills, or separate audio transcription and OCR costs.You can start building today by grabbing an API key in Google AI Studio, trying our Doorstep Parcels, Speed Sketch, and Find the Zoo Keeper demo apps, and following the Python, JavaScript, and REST guides in the Decisions API documentation.Ecosystem integrations are rolling out across OpenRouter, LangChain, Vercel, LiteLLM, Pydantic AI, Pipecat, LiveKit, and OpenCode alongside the google-genai SDKs, with support coming soon to Gemini in Google Cloud.

articles.sourceTitle: I'm making LLMs work on small and old devices
articles.title: hyperionaidev/smolmaxxing: maxxing the ability to run different LLMs on the smallest devices possible · GitHub
articles.text:
Every device around you is more capable than it looks. TV boxes, old phones, single-board computers and routers all ship with CPUs, RAM and flash that sit idle most of the day. smolmaxxing is about unlocking that capability: finding the biggest language model each device can really run, then pushing it further with custom kernels, smarter memory use and weight streaming. Every claim is measured on the hardware itself.
Device #1 is a Xiaomi TV Box S (3rd Gen): Amlogic S7D, 4× Cortex-A55 @ 2.5 GHz, 1.9 GB of RAM (about 1 GB usable), eMMC flash, Android 14, no root. On it, this repo runs models from 260 K to 16 B parameters:

Qwen3.5-0.8B: 16.8 tok/s (2.2× the stock 7.5; measured in the evening of 11-05, see §17).
Qwen3.5-2B: 7.7 tok/s in real chat. The box's speed drifts by ~10 % over a day, so every step is measured back to back: §16 gave +11 %, §17 another +7 %.
An 8B mixture-of-experts model (Moon-Beam-8B-A1B): 7.2 tok/s in real chat, its experts paged from flash on demand and prefetched one layer ahead (§19).
A dense 1-bit 8B model (Bonsai-8B): 5.2 tok/s in real chat, up from 1.2: fully resident in a "headless" mode plus a lookup-table kernel (§19).
A 16B mixture-of-experts model (Ling-mini-2.0): 5.1 tok/s in real chat, coherent over 600-word answers, the same expert pager applied unchanged (§20). Twice Moon-Beam's size, but not better per byte: bigger only helps on this box when the model is also better.
A dense 9B model: 0.27 tok/s, streaming most of its weights from flash.

Device #2 is a first-generation iPad Air (2013): Apple A7, 2 cores, NEON without dotprod, 1 GB of RAM, iOS 12.5.7, jailbroken, CPU only. A 13-year-old tablet runs a 1.7B-parameter model at 24-26 tok/s (18-22 in long chats), a 4B one at about 10 tok/s, an 8B mixture of experts at about 3.5 tok/s (5 with half its experts, at a quality cost), and a 16B one at 2.6-4.5 tok/s, with their experts paged from flash, from a chat page in its own Safari. See Results on device #2.
Every step is written up experiment by experiment in EXPERIMENT.md (E1-E160).

"First run" is the first time each model ran on the box:

0.8B: the stock Q4_K_M file.
2B: the stock file, streamed from flash because it didn't fit in RAM. Its first build that fit ran at 4.8, so from there the gain is ×1.6.
4B: the stock file, which thrashed.
8B dense: the last 0.1 GB streamed from flash.
8B MoE: the first expert-pager run, without routing bias.
9B: streamed.
16B: started on the Moon-Beam recipe, so its gain is small.

On this box, the 2B is the best speed-quality balance. Ling-mini-2.0 shows that bigger isn't automatically better: it is twice Moon-Beam's size, but scores worse per byte and runs slower.

Granite 4.0 H 1B was the one model close to the 2B's quality. Rebuilt our way (E62), it runs at 5.29 tok/s, below the 2B's 6.55 at slightly lower quality: it carries about twice the 0.8B's weight bytes per token.
Physics of the box: one process can hold ~0.96 GB before Android starts killing things (~1.15 GB in headless mode, with the launchers and Google services force-stopped), and flash reads top out at 278 MB/s, with a lone ~1 MB random read costing ~6 ms. A model that has to stream X MB per token can never beat 278 / X tokens per second. That, not the CPU, is what limits everything above 2B, and why a mixture-of-experts model, which touches ~1 B of its 8 B weights per token, is the way past it.
10 tok/s at 8 B? Measured, not guessed (E98): Moon-Beam reaches 10.4 tok/s with 2 experts per token, but the text turns to gibberish; the best coherent setting is ~7-8 tok/s. Dense Qwen3-8B is Bonsai-8B at 1 bit, and the smallest Qwen MoE (35B-A3B) touches 3× Moon-Beam's weights per token.
